newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Two pct of infotechnology said delaying trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Two pct of infotechnology said delaying trade deal.

text.p: Talks to remove tariffs under an information technology agreement (ITA) in Singapore this week focus on four types of products covering only two percent of the industry's global exports, officials said.

These four categories -- fibre optics, graphics display tubes, photocopiers and capacitors, which are circuits used in electronic goods -- represented only $13 billion of the $595 billion worth of IT products exported last year.
But officials say consensus on these issues is vital for any IT deal to be struck at the first ministerial meeting of the 128-nation World Trade Organisation (WTO), which runs until December 13.
The European Union (EU) wants these products included in any IT agreement. The United States wants them left out.
"The work is going on in the back rooms to get this settled," a European source told Reuters.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters on Sunday evening that U.S. and EU officials had met to try to thrash out the differences which would eliminate tariffs on computer and telecommunications technology by 2000.
"We are making some very important progress," Barshefsky said. "The work is going on quite intensively. It will remain intense throughout the week."
U.S. and EU officials said a series of intense bilateral discussions would be held this week in hopes of winning a deal.
Both sides have traded swipes at each other over the ITA talks as the negotiations continue.

Barshefsky expressed concern on Sunday about Europe's commitment to the agreement. EU officials have, in turn, accused the U.S. of wanting to exclude the four key types of products to protect their own domestic industry.
The Americans were in the pocket of industry and had brought industry lobbyists with them to Singapore, a European source said.
The EU argues that the four categories must be included because they are all key information technology (IT) products.
"Of total world exports of IT products of $13 billion, the EU exports $2.6 billion and imports $4.1 billion," said the European source.
"We are not doing it to defend exports -- we actually have a deficit in these products," he said.
The EU accuses the U.S. of caving in to pressure from Xerox Corp over the exclusion of photocopiers and from Corning over fibre optics.
U.S. sources say Corning has waged an effective lobbying campaign in the U.S. Congress for several months.
"We were also lobbied by Xerox and told them to go away," said one European diplomat.
But the U.S. rejects such criticism, saying the four categories all contain products that are not central to the burgeoning IT industry.
They said every country in the negotiations wanted to exclude some products and add that the area of disagreement covered a minute part of overall trade.
Both sides hope a deal can be struck this week.
